answers.explanation: If the answer is cached and its TTL hasn't run out, nobody else needs to be asked.
That's a referral. Caching it means the next lookup in marshall.edu can skip the root and edu servers.
The resolver follows the alias by restarting with the canonical name, starting with its cache.
That's what makes DNS resilient: zones have several nameservers, and a broken one is just skipped.
Recursive: "get me the answer." The resolver then makes iterative queries to the root, TLD, and authoritative servers.
Root and TLD servers only give referrals; they don't do recursive lookups for anyone.
It saves work: a mistyped name that a program keeps retrying would otherwise go to the authoritative servers every time. The resolver algorithm caches errors too.
Root, TLD, authoritative: one level of the tree each.
The `.com` and `.net` delegations have long TTLs, so a busy resolver asks the root only occasionally.
